H1.idea: Prices wobble around a slow-moving level, so averaging the last few days should beat using the latest price.
H1.result: Averaging made the guess worse: errors were 10% to 60% bigger than just using the latest price.

H2.idea: A price that changed recently is more likely to change again.
H2.result: Using this beat the organisers' baseline by 0.08 on the practice dates. On its own it did not clearly hold on the held-back weeks (+0.03); it did as part of a mix.

H3.idea: Most series are only two or three months old, so borrow history from similar series.
H3.result: +0.045 over the baseline, but only because it fills in for series too new for the baseline to handle.

H4.idea: When a price jumps because a provider joined or left, it drifts back afterwards.
H4.result: It mostly stays where it jumped to. Providers that leave almost never return within a week (0% to 6%).

H5.idea: The most recent day's data gets revised later.
H5.result: We only have one copy of the data, so there is nothing to compare.

H6.idea: Off-the-shelf forecasting models (Chronos, TimesFM) cannot say where these prices go, but may judge how uncertain they are.
H6.result: Their guess of the price itself was worse than the baseline. Their sense of how wide the range should be was good: +0.12 over the baseline on the held-back weeks.

H7.idea: The same GPU's price on another data source moves first.
H7.result: Nudging our guess by the other source's last move never helped.

H7b.idea: If many prices on a data source changed lately, each one will move more next.

H9.idea: After a jump of more than 5%, the price gives some of it back within a week.
H9.result: Betting on a pullback made things slightly worse.

H10.idea: A burst of news headlines about GPU price rises (found with Exa) warns of a jump.
H10.result: A tiny gain (+0.01) that came from a single episode. It hurt on more dates than it helped.

H11.idea: Each published price is the middle of a short list of provider offers, so every move comes from a provider changing its price, joining or leaving.
H11.result: We can rebuild the published price exactly from the offers. 86% of moves are a provider repricing and 10% are a provider joining or leaving, but joining and leaving caused about a third of our forecast error. The size of those jumps can be read off the list.

H12.idea: Simulate the list of offers and take its middle, instead of extrapolating the price.
H12.result: The first version only tied our starting model (0.170 against 0.169). It could not foresee brand-new providers joining.

H13.idea: Big price changes are announced publicly before they happen.
H13.result: Only 2 of the 37 biggest were announced ahead (Nebius 15 days, Jarvislabs 10 days). Most big moves are marketplace prices that nobody announces.

H14.idea: Our ranges are steadily too narrow on the upside, so widen them automatically.
H14.result: The misses came in one stretch of several weeks, not steadily. Automatic widening helped in that stretch and hurt before it.

H15.idea: Learn which method to trust more as results come in.
H15.result: Learned weights were no better than a plain average (+0.004). The best method keeps changing, and chasing it loses.

H16.idea: Predict whether a price will move, then how far.
H16.result: We can tell fairly well whether a price will move, but not which way. The forecaster built on it lost (0.108 against 0.169).

H17.idea: The Laya decision model can read a price history and say up, flat or down.
H17.result: Worse than always guessing the most common outcome, even after recalibration. A simple statistical model on the same numbers did far better. Fine-tuning did not finish because it ran out of memory.

H18.idea: A pretrained model's sense of uncertainty carries over because it reacts to how jumpy the last couple of weeks were.
H18.result: Giving it only the last 16 days works best. Mixed with our starting model it scored 0.170 against 0.112 on the held-back weeks, and it passes the stricter check.

H19.idea: When two data sources disagree on a GPU's price, the gap closes.
H19.result: It does not close in any predictable way. No outside price index helped either.

H20.idea: Have an AI write a tiny model's weights by hand (weight-space programming) instead of training it.
H20.result: The hand-written weights beat the same model trained the normal way, but did not clearly beat our starting model.

H21.idea: Find past situations that looked like today, across all 592 series, and see what happened next.
H21.result: +0.03 on the practice dates and +0.02 on the held-back weeks when mixed with the starting model. A stricter check says the held-back result could be luck (about a 1 in 7 chance). The thing that matters most is how many providers are in the list.

H22.idea: A model built for small tables (TabPFN) beats our tree model.
H22.result: We stopped it: the laptop was out of memory and this was the least promising heavy job. This says nothing about the method.

H23.idea: A series that never moves should get no range at all.
H23.result: A small but steady gain (+0.008) across all series. Fancier rules per price type looked great early and fell apart later.

H24.idea: Give each provider's offer that provider's own recent pricing habits, then take the middle of the list.
H24.result: The first method to predict the price itself better than assuming no change (5% less error, 10% less where a frequent repricer sits in the middle). Mixed with the starting model it scored 0.185 against 0.112 on the held-back weeks, and it passes the stricter check.

H25.idea: Skip the simulation: just look up who sits in the middle of the list and how often they change price.
H25.result: Tied the starting model. There are too few past examples to learn from. Simulating works, looking up does not.

H26.idea: A provider's published pricing policy (found with Exa) tells us how often its price will move.
H26.result: Assuming a provider never changes price was a better first guess. Verda says it is ending dynamic pricing but still changes prices on 4 days in 10.

H27.idea: Build a calendar of announced price changes with Exa and apply each one on its date.
H27.result: 17 of 17 announced prices showed up exactly as announced. A big gain on the practice dates (0.283 against 0.209), but from just two announcements, and it could not be checked on the held-back weeks. It is switched off in our submission.

H28.idea: Put the edges of our range where the price would land if one provider left or joined.
H28.result: 0.219 against 0.112 on the held-back weeks, our biggest single gain, though a stricter check calls it borderline. Providers change in batches: right after one change, another is over 20 times more likely.

H29.idea: Rental prices fall with a chip's age at a steady rate that we can extend two to three years.
H29.result: Assuming no change beat it over the past year, because prices rose in 2026 (a shortage year).

H30.idea: A provider that lists a GPU on one data source will soon show up on the other.
H30.result: It is 17 times more likely than chance, but that is still about a 0.3% chance per day. Not enough to forecast with.

H31.idea: Our new methods fixed what they were aimed at, and what is left is mostly new providers joining.
H31.result: Error from frequent repricers fell the most. The biggest remaining causes: a new offer joining (29%), frequent repricers (16%), announced one-off changes (14%).

H32.idea: The provider simulation still holds up if a price trend suddenly stops or reverses.
H32.result: In made-up scenarios it kept most of its lead (+0.033 to +0.035, against +0.040 in the real data). We have not seen a real reversal yet.

H33.idea: A provider's price change shows up on one data source a day before the other.
H33.result: Checked before building anything: it happens in only 1 case in 3, and price gaps between sources do not close.

H34.idea: An equal mix of all seven working methods beats the baseline on weeks it has never seen.
H34.result: 0.214 against 0.084 on the 37 scored series, and 0.228 against 0.102 on every other series, which nothing was tuned on. 80% of prices landed inside our range, and the goal is 80%.

H35.idea: The provider simulation also works for the big clouds (AWS, Google, Azure, Oracle).
H35.result: With about 450 offers per list, the individual moves cancel out. Their list prices almost never change, so giving them no range is right, and our submission already does that.

H36.idea: We can give useful two to three year ranges for H100 and A100 rent and resale.
H36.result: Ranges, yes: H100 rent is $3.49 now and about $2.31 in two years ($1.21 to $4.17). Proven accuracy, no: nothing beat assuming no change when tested on the past.

H37.result: An independent check found one tiny leak, now fixed (it moved forecasts by 0.002% at most). It confirmed our scoring matches the organisers'. It also showed that some of our claims about the held-back weeks were too confident.
